title: The Definitive Guide to Setting Up Your AI Second Brain
author: Vicky Zhao
summary: Argues that people conflate three distinct brains — human, AI, and the shared second brain — and get confused about what belongs where. Human thinking is powered by experience, curiosity, taste and judgment and must not be outsourced; the AI brain is excellent at doing but produces generic slop when asked to think without curated context. The shared second brain is the context layer that powers both, and it therefore has to be physically split: a thinking folder (bottom-up, Zettelkasten, human-only) and a doing folder (top-down, hierarchical, AI-facing). Two golden rules follow — never mix human and AI output, and never let doing distract from thinking.
takeaways: Three brains, three jobs: human brain = thinking (powered by experience, taste, judgment); AI brain = doing (workflows, execution); shared second brain = the context that powers both.
Two golden rules for the vault: never mix human and AI output, and never let 'doing' (to-dos, project management) crowd out 'thinking'. Every space should have its own purpose.
The split is physical: a Zettelkasten/Thinking folder that is hers alone, and an AI-context/Doing folder that agents read.
Zettelkasten ('note box') was popularised by Niklas Luhmann, who used 90,000+ notes to produce 70+ books and 400+ academic articles.

Three Zettelkasten principles: atomic notes (one note, one idea), connected notes (a web linking new-to-new and new-to-old), and processing — rephrasing in your own words and distilling a precise title.
She deviates from the classic three-tier system (fleeting / literature / permanent), collapsing the first two into 'raw notes' processed straight into permanent ones.

The doing folder needs five components: About Me (preferences, standards, dislikes, goals), Frameworks (your own decision heuristics as SOPs), Examples (good AND bad), Knowledge base, and a Knowledge map indexing it.
Critiques Andrej Karpathy's 'LLM wiki': fine for doing tasks, unsuitable as a full second brain, because letting AI process your notes means you never process them yourself.
The doing folder is a closed loop: AI output → filed back as a good/bad example → knowledge base grows → knowledge map re-indexes → context compounds.
quotes: I would argue that the AI brain is amazing at doing things.
We don't want to outsource the thinking that's core to our human brain but we can outsource a lot of the doing that... doesn't really bring any value.

The biggest mistake I see with people building second brains is they're just trying to catalog everything that they know or they find interesting and then you don't do anything to help augment how you actually think.
AI is a great student, right? is like this smart PhD student who's going to be able to understand your frameworks and be able to apply it to his work... it is also a good apprentice.
You can't just complain that... this is BS but then not be able to bring something better.
I do not suggest that you use the LLM wiki as your shared second brain because it's missing so many different parts of the type of processing that you want to do.
bestIdeas: The thinking/doing split as a filing rule — a mechanical test ('did I form this, or did AI produce it?') that transfers to any AI-augmented note system.
Show, don't just tell: pairing a written rule with labelled good AND bad examples closes the interpretation gap that language alone leaves. Applies to any agent context or prompt.
Frameworks as the bridge artefact between human judgment and AI scale — it is your own heuristics, not generic ones, that should become agent skills.
The compounding context loop: output filed back as an example means the system improves without a separate curation chore.
Evaluating a popular AI workflow against whether it serves thinking or doing, before adopting it wholesale.
tools: Obsidian — the markdown vault holding both the thinking and doing sides.
Claude Code, Codex — named as the agents that would read the doing folder.
Zettelkasten — the note-taking method for the thinking side.
Idea Compass — her own note-stretching template, covered in another video.
method: Split the vault into two top-level folders: Thinking (human, bottom-up, Zettelkasten) and Doing (AI, top-down, hierarchical).
Thinking note anatomy: a title distilling the atomic idea; a body in your own words; a link to the source note; links to related notes. Tags and metadata optional.
Doing folder — About Me: identity, preferences, standards (e.g. 'don't use em dashes'), goals and vision.
Doing folder — Frameworks: your distilled SOPs and decision rules (Eisenhower matrix, or her own effort vs delegate-ability matrix), which become agent skills or slash commands.
Doing folder — Examples: good and bad, tied to the criteria in the frameworks.
Doing folder — Knowledge base: the onboarding-folder equivalent for a new employee.
Doing folder — Knowledge map: an index describing where everything in the knowledge base lives.

keyMessage: Keep human thinking and AI doing physically separate in the vault, so the tool augments your cognition instead of contaminating it, while still giving AI the curated context it needs to avoid generic output.
